units.text: The Mirbad and the Building of the Medina Mosque
How did the mirbad become a mosque?

The camel knelt at a mirbad in Medina. Ibn Ishaq recounts the question about the land and the offer to make it a mosque; Anas describes the Banu al-Najjar’s reply and the preparation of the site. The Muslims then took part in building it.
From the Camel to the Mirbad

In the Sira of Ibn Hisham, Ibn Ishaq describes the camel kneeling at a mirbad in the quarter of the Banu Malik ibn al-Najjar, then rising, going a little way, and returning to its first resting place. He says that the mirbad belonged to Sahl and Suhayl, two orphans in the care of Muadh ibn Afra. The account continues with the Prophet ﷺ dismounting and his baggage being carried to the house of Abu Ayyub.

The Prophet ﷺ asked, “Whose is the mirbad?” Muadh replied that it belonged to the two boys, said he would satisfy them for it, and proposed that it be made a mosque. This question and offer occur in Ibn Ishaq’s report; they are not the text of an agreement on a specific price.
The Reply of the Banu al-Najjar

In Sahih Muslim, Anas recounts the journey from the Banu Amr ibn Awf to the courtyard of Abu Ayyub; the Prophet ﷺ prayed wherever the time for prayer overtook him, including in sheepfolds. Then he ordered a mosque to be built and asked the leading men of the Banu al-Najjar to name him a price for their enclosed plot. They replied that they sought its price only from God.
The group’s answer remains theirs in Anas’s report, while Ibn Ishaq names the two boys and puts the offer in Muadh’s mouth. Neither of these passages tells us how much was actually paid.
Preparing the Ground

The report does not begin with walls already standing: Anas lists date palms, graves of polytheists, and ruins in the enclosed plot, and says that the Prophet ﷺ ordered the palms cut down, the graves dug up, and the ruins levelled. The digging up in this report concerns specifically the graves mentioned there.

The account in Muslim continues: the date palms were set in a row toward the qibla, and the two doorposts of the mosque were made of stone. Muslim also preserves a short report of the Prophet ﷺ praying in sheepfolds before the mosque was built, followed by a parallel transmission referring to a similar report, without a new detailed text.
The Workers and Their Words

Ibn Ishaq says that the Prophet ﷺ worked on the mosque and that the Emigrants and Helpers worked alongside him. In the continuation of Anas’s report in Muslim, the workers recited rajaz verse, with the Prophet ﷺ among them; their words turn to the good of the Hereafter and a prayer for the Helpers and Emigrants.

In the Sira a verse by an unnamed Muslim urges work while the Prophet ﷺ is working. The Sira also recounts the Muslims’ recitation of rajaz and their prayer for the good of the Hereafter and mercy for the Helpers and Emigrants. It then distinguishes Ibn Hisham’s literary comment that those words are not rajaz, before transmitting a saying of the Prophet ﷺ in different wording.
Who Is Addressing Whom?

In the Sira of Ibn Hisham, Muadh identifies the boys and offers to satisfy them; in Muslim, the Banu al-Najjar answer the Prophet ﷺ after his request for a price for the enclosed plot. In Urwa’s account in al-Bukhari, the name of the boys’ guardian differs, and they offer to give the plot as a gift. These passages do not state a specific price.

In al-Bayhaqi’s transmission from al-Zuhri through Musa ibn Uqba, the boys are in the care of As’ad ibn Zurara. It is said that As’ad offered them date palms of his in Banu Bayada in exchange for their mirbad, but they replied that they would give it to the Prophet ﷺ. It is also said that the Prophet ﷺ bought the mirbad from them. In Anas’s report, the Banu al-Najjar respond to a request to set a price for the enclosure.

A marginal note in the edition of Muslim, not Anas’s account, reports through Ibn Sad from al-Waqidi that the Prophet ﷺ bought the mirbad from them for ten dinars, which Abu Bakr paid on his behalf. Ibn Hajar relates a legal argument about sale by a non-owner, then a possible reply: the Prophet ﷺ may have bargained with the boys themselves, with their paternal uncle, in whose care they were, joining the bargaining. In this possible answer, the boys belong to the Banu al-Najjar.
Building materials and stages

In Ibn Hajar’s explanation, labin means unfired mud bricks. He cites Ibn Aidh on a stage when the mosque was an open shelter before it was roofed, and al-Zubayr on palm fronds followed by mud bricks, with different timing.

Muslim's brief report mentions the Prophet ﷺ praying in sheepfolds before the mosque was built; a parallel transmission refers to the same report without further detail. In Anas's longer account, prayer comes before the order to build the mosque, followed by preparation of the site.
Voices of the Rajaz and Its Commentary

Anas’s report attributes the words of supplication to the workers reciting rajaz with the Messenger of God ﷺ among them. The Sira speaks of the Muslims, then gives a distinct phrase transmitted by Ibn Ishaq from the Prophet ﷺ. Other verses, in Ibn Hajar’s transmission from al-Zubayr, are attributed to an unnamed Muslim and to Ali.

Ibn Hajar discusses al-Zuhri’s limitation to what reached him and the dispute over rajaz and poetry, explaining the difference between composing and reciting. Ibn Hisham’s comment on the Muslims’ words about life in the Hereafter is a literary comment in his own name, not the Prophet’s words.

go out every morning to the harra, waiting for him until the midday heat drove them back. One day, after waiting a long time, they returned home. When they had gone to their houses, a Jewish man climbed onto one of their fortified buildings to look at something. He caught sight of the Messenger of God ﷺ and his companions dressed in white, wavering in the mirage. The man could not help but cry out at the top of his voice: “People of the Arabs, here is the one you have been waiting for—your good fortune!” The Muslims sprang to their weapons and met the Messenger of God ﷺ on the open ground of the harra. He turned them to the right until he brought them to stay among the Banu Amr ibn Awf, on a Monday in the month of Rabi al-Awwal. Abu Bakr stood before the people and the Messenger of God ﷺ sat silently. Some of the Helpers arriving who had never seen the Messenger of God ﷺ began greeting Abu Bakr; then the sun fell on the Messenger of God ﷺ, and Abu Bakr came and shaded him with his cloak. At that point the people recognized the Messenger of God ﷺ. He stayed among the Banu Amr ibn Awf for somewhat more than ten nights. The mosque founded on piety was established, and the Messenger of God ﷺ prayed in it.

The answer to the first objection is that the majority hold rajaz to be a type of poetry when it is metrical. It has been said that when he ﷺ spoke those words he did not leave the rhyme ending uninflected, but pronounced its final t with a vowel; this is not established. A report from Sahl ibn Sad about the Battle of the Trench will follow with the wording “so forgive the Emigrants and the Helpers,” which is not metrical. The answer to the second objection is that what was precluded for him ﷺ was composing poetry, not reciting it, and there is no evidence forbidding him from reciting a quotation of it.
